title: Love and awe (Yesodei HaTorah 2:2)
hookLine: contemplating the wonders of creation leads to love and awe
last: FIRST, KNOW THERE IS A FIRST BEING.

cards: The Torah commands love: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart." It also commands awe, or fear. But a feeling is a strange thing to command.

Nobody can be ordered into loving someone. So Maimonides asks, right there in his code, in the second chapter: what is the way to love God, and to stand in awe? His answer doesn't begin with a prayer or a rule.
It begins with looking at the world.

teach.b: Love and awe. In Hebrew, ahavah and yirah.

His answer, in plain English: when a person thinks carefully about God's great and wondrous works and creatures, and sees in them a wisdom with no measure and no end, that person at once loves, and praises, and longs to know.
Love doesn't come from willpower. It comes from attention. Look closely at how a thing is made, and something in you moves toward its maker.
The person thirsts, he says, borrowing from the Psalms: "My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God." Second, the turn. Keep looking, and the same thoughts bring you up short.
You step back, a small creature with a little knowledge, before a wisdom without limit. That is awe, and again he reaches for a psalm: "What is man, that Thou art mindful of him?" Third, the pairing.
One act of attention produces both.
Love draws you closer. Awe makes you step back. He holds them together, like breathing in and breathing out.
His code goes on to describe the world as the science of his day understood it: the spheres, the stars, the elements. Some of that science has not lasted.
The method has: learn how the world works, and let what you learn lead to wonder. For Maimonides, studying creation isn't a distraction from the religious life. It's one of its doors.

how: Jews who study Maimonides read Yesodei HaTorah 2:2 as a guide to the commandments to love and to fear God, and some take it as a reason to study the natural world as part of a religious life.

o: two feelings to be kept hidden during prayer
a pair of blessings said at the Shabbat table
drawing near and stepping back, from looking closely

games.q: love and awe — tap the pairs.

s: Maimonides says love of God comes from forcing yourself to feel it
he says it comes from contemplating God's works and seeing their wisdom.
in his account, the same act of looking leads to both love and awe
love draws a person near; the same thoughts make them step back in awe.
Maimonides quotes the Psalms to describe this longing
"My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God."

games.q: the Torah commands you to love God. you can't order yourself to feel something. what does Maimonides say to do?
o: repeat the command until the feeling comes.
look closely at creation and see its wisdom.
wait until love arrives on its own.
games.why: he says contemplating God's great and wondrous works leads straight to love, and then, as you keep looking, to awe.

practice: Look closely at one natural thing, a leaf, a stone, your own hand, as if you'd never seen one before: its edges, its lines, how it's put together. Notice if something moves toward it, a little warmth, a little delight.
Then notice the other movement, the step back before how much you don't know, and let both be there.

wordCard.voice: Love and awe. Ahavah and yirah: for Maimonides, the two movements that come from looking closely at creation, drawing near and standing back. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: love and awe (or fear), the pair Maimonides joins in Yesodei HaTorah 2:2.

carryVoice: Your line: love and awe. One look, two movements: closer, and back. That's one thousand one hundred forty-four days.
